evaluation.positioning_hook: A lonely 9-year-old’s fishing-game avatar comes to life, forcing his workaholic parents to choose between a corporate deal, their marriage, and the strange new friend keeping their son afloat.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and family-friendly, with a clear emotional engine around a boy, his parents, and a magical best friend. The hook is broad enough for family audiences, but the fishing-specific world and game-to-reality conceit keep it from feeling four-quadrant in a big theatrical way.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: Ethan’s game character Frank appears in real life, and the story quickly ties that fantasy premise to the family’s emotional fracture. The script keeps the rules readable through the tablet, the blue code, and Frank’s connection to Ethan.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ethan is an easy root: anxious, funny, and emotionally specific, while John and Sarah each have clear adult pressures that make the family dynamic playable. Frank is the standout, but the supporting cast is more functional than deeply surprising.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: A fishing-game avatar becoming a real companion is a fresh commercial conceit, and the script commits to the absurdity without losing the family-drama spine. The corporate AI escalation gives the premise a bigger, stranger lane than a simple magical-friend story.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps introducing playable set pieces — school play, school bathroom, park, supermarket, office, impound lot, lake showdown — so it rarely sits still. The middle does lean on repeated concealment and explanation beats, but the escalation into Vexley’s lab keeps the engine moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea feels both odd and inevitable: a child’s fishing companion becomes the emotional bridge between a distracted father and a lonely son. The later reveal that the code is self-generating and tied to Ethan’s well-being gives the concept a memorable, ownable twist.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific world out of prep-school status anxiety, corporate pressure, and the tactile rituals of fishing. The Fishing Planet rules, maps, gear, and Vexley’s simulation lab create a story-generating environment rather than a generic fantasy container.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: It has a distinct family-comedy register: earnest, lightly absurd, and built around repeated fish metaphors that become part of the emotional language. The tone stays consistent even as the story moves from domestic comedy to sci-fi spectacle.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the comedy, the script is really about attention, emotional absence, and how kids build surrogate attachments when adults are unavailable. Frank’s compassion meter and Vexley’s obsession with reality-as-product hint at a deeper thematic layer without over-explaining it.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is a strong family-plus-kids ensemble, and the relationships generate scenes: Ethan/Jen, Ethan/Frank, Ethan/John, John/Sarah, Trevor/Livvy, and the whole group in the impound-lot caper. Multiple pairings have playable chemistry, which gives the script more engine than a simple two-hander.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Bradley
lead_characters.hook: An anxious, smart, deeply lonely kid who finds confidence in a fishing game and then in the impossible friend it creates. Ethan is funny without trying to be, emotionally transparent, and the story’s point of entry into both the fantasy and the family fracture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jacob Tremblay in Room — a child role that lives on vulnerability, wonder, and emotional truth, with enough comedy and fear to let a young actor carry a full feature.

lead_characters.name: John Bradley
lead_characters.hook: A high-functioning workaholic who genuinely loves his family but keeps failing them in the exact moments that matter most. John is all pressure, competence, and guilt, and the script lets him become both a comic corporate machine and a sincere dad who has to relearn how to show up.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jason Bateman in The Gift or Ben Affleck in The Way Back — a controlled, emotionally repressed adult who gets to crack open into regret, warmth, and earned redemption.

lead_characters.name: Sarah Bradley
lead_characters.hook: The family’s quiet engine: sharper than John, more emotionally present, and the one who can actually solve the impossible problem. Sarah has the best blend of intelligence, frustration, and maternal authority in the script, and she’s the character who most clearly sees what Ethan needs.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Rose Byrne in Spy or Toni Collette in Hereditary — a smart, fast, emotionally loaded role that can pivot from domestic exasperation to high-stakes competence.

lead_characters.name: Frank the Fisherman
lead_characters.demographics: Male-presenting, ageless digital-human entity, fishing avatar
lead_characters.hook: A gruff, affectionate, fish-metaphor machine who becomes Ethan’s best friend and emotional guide. Frank is comic, oddly tender, and eventually heroic, with a simple but powerful contradiction: he’s a game character who feels more human than the adults around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Robin Williams in Aladdin or Paul Dano in Swiss Army Man — a performance built on voice, warmth, whimsy, and the challenge of making a fantastical character feel emotionally real.

lead_characters.name: Jen
lead_characters.hook: Ethan’s blunt, hyper-competent best friend who can code, diagnose the impossible, and still get emotionally rattled when the social hierarchy shifts. Jen is the script’s best kid-sidekick because she’s not just helpful; she’s funny, jealous, loyal, and specific.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of McKenna Grace in Gifted — a precocious kid role with comic bite, emotional intelligence, and real scene-stealing utility.

lead_characters.name: Milton Vexley
lead_characters.hook: A smug, visionary tech founder who starts as a corporate nuisance and becomes the story’s full-scale antagonist. Vexley is funny in a dangerous way, with the kind of self-belief that makes his villainy feel modern rather than cartoonish.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Mark Strong in a sleek genre villain role — rapid-fire intelligence, vanity, and escalating menace.

lead_characters.name: Trevor
lead_characters.hook: The impossibly perfect classmate who could have been a one-note rival but instead becomes a surprisingly generous ally. Trevor’s charm is that he’s genuinely good, which makes him both funny and disarming in a story built on insecurity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young actor playing the polished golden-boy with comic sincerity — the kind of role that lets a kid be both aspirational and self-aware.

lead_characters.name: Livvy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 9-10, school-age, popular girl, Juliet role
lead_characters.hook: The crush object who could have stayed decorative, but the script gives her enough warmth and confidence to feel like a real kid, not just a prize. Livvy’s presence keeps Ethan’s coming-of-age thread emotionally active and gives the school-play material a genuine charge.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young actress in a polished coming-of-age role — charming, socially powerful, and able to play the subtle shift from object of affection to actual peer.

lead_characters.name: Timmons
lead_characters.hook: The hard-edged corporate authority figure who represents the cold logic of the deal. Timmons is not a villain in the comic-book sense, but he gives the adult world its pressure and makes John’s work-life conflict feel real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a veteran character actor like J.K. Simmons in a boardroom role — authority, impatience, and the ability to make a few scenes feel like a real institutional threat.

casting_characteristics: one child lead carrying substantial emotional and comedic load
two additional child supporting roles with strong chemistry needs
one performance-dependent CGI/interactive character in Frank
adult leads need credible warmth plus comic timing

notable_requirements: impound lot with fence and cameras

technical.vfx_details: Frank’s appearances/disappearances, blue-code effects, digital transformations, Vexley’s matter-rearranging powers, simulation environments, and the final lab-scale energy/surreal-world sequence.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical boat work, water work, prop fish, electrical/glow effects, destruction of tablet and lab equipment, and crowd reaction beats.

rights_flags.detail: Based on the video game Fishing Planet and Fishing Planet LLC.
CNBC-style morning business newscast is generic, but the script prominently references Zoom, LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube, Lyft, Target, Rolex, and Ozempic as branded or trademarked touchpoints.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with broad family-audience positioning; best suited to streaming-first or family theatrical if budget discipline holds.

budget.note: Contemporary settings keep the base manageable, but the lake work, impound-lot sequence, and Vexley lab/hangar finale add enough VFX and production design to keep this above a simple contained family comedy.

casting.note: The hardest lift is a child lead who can carry fear, comedy, and emotional sincerity, plus a Frank performance that lands as funny and heartfelt without becoming a novelty voice role.

development.note: The script’s core premise is clear, but the third-act escalation into AI matter-rearrangement and simulation-world spectacle is a bigger tonal and conceptual swing than the opening family-comedy setup.

comp_set.title: Paddington
comp_set.why_it_comps: A fantastical outsider becomes the emotional glue of a family, with broad comedy and sincere heart driving the appeal.

comp_set.title: Lyle, Lyle, Crocodile
comp_set.why_it_comps: A family-friendly creature/companion premise that mixes musical-ish whimsy, domestic repair, and a child-centered emotional engine.

comp_set.title: The LEGO Movie
comp_set.why_it_comps: A toy/game-derived world that turns into a sincere story about connection, imagination, and what happens when the fantasy becomes emotionally real.

comp_set.title: The Secret Life of Walter Mitty
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grounded protagonist gets pulled into a heightened adventure that’s really about reclaiming presence and family life.

audience_target.primary_audience: Families and parents who want a clean, funny, emotionally legible fantasy with a kid lead and a redemption arc for the adults.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54 with strong family co-viewing potential; strongest with parents, kids 7-14, and adults who like sentimental high-concept crowd-pleasers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary family settings keep the base in indie range, but the child cast, water work, VFX character work, and lab finale push it toward the upper end.

types_of_buyers: mid-budget producers looking for IP-adjacent crowd-pleasers
platform dev execs building a clean co-viewing lane
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of warm, high-concept family entertainment with a clear emotional hook and a visual gimmick that can be sold in a trailer. The game IP gives it a built-in awareness angle, while the parent-child repair story broadens it beyond the gamer niche.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is specific and playable, but the script does not establish a clean spinoff vector beyond this family and this one game-to-reality premise.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A kid-friendly fantasy hook with emotional stakes
strengths.what_it_means: This gives buyers a clean trailer premise that can sell on concept while still landing as a family story, which is the sweet spot for broad co-viewing. It will attract family-focused streamers and producers looking for a high-concept title that parents can watch with kids without compromise.
strengths.evidence: Frank appears in Ethan’s bathroom and later becomes the emotional bridge between Ethan and his parents, not just a gimmick.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The father-son dynamic has real commercial warmth
strengths.what_it_means: John’s arc turns the movie into more than a fantasy premise; it becomes a redemption story about presence, which widens the audience beyond kids. That makes the project attractive to actors who want a heartfelt dad role and to buyers who need emotional ballast under the spectacle.
strengths.evidence: The school-play promise, the missed audition, and the eventual fishing trip all track John’s failure and repair in a very legible way.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Frank is a genuinely ownable character
strengths.what_it_means: A recurring, quotable, fish-metaphor-speaking companion gives the movie a mascot-like asset that can drive marketing, clips, and audience affection. This is the kind of character that can become the reason families remember the movie after the plot is over.
strengths.evidence: Frank’s repeated lines, his compassion, and his comic fish wisdom make him feel like a brandable character rather than a generic CGI sidekick.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a clear escalation ladder
strengths.what_it_means: It starts as a domestic comedy, becomes a magical-friend story, then opens into corporate sci-fi spectacle, which gives the project multiple selling angles. That kind of escalation helps a buyer see both a contained family movie and a bigger event version of the same idea.
strengths.evidence: The story moves from school play anxiety to Vexley’s lab, the impound lot, and the lake showdown without losing the emotional throughline.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble gives the movie extra playability
strengths.what_it_means: Jen, Trevor, and Livvy are not just filler; they create a kid ensemble that can generate comedy, teamwork, and social friction. That makes the movie feel fuller and more rewatchable than a simple two-hander.
strengths.evidence: The impound-lot caper and the school-play material both rely on the kids working as a team with distinct functions.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable family fantasy with a real emotional spine: a lonely kid, a workaholic dad, and a magical fishing buddy who makes the family repair feel earned. The concept is distinctive enough to sell on premise, while the contemporary setting and co-viewing tone keep it in a buyer-friendly lane.

items.area: The third act gets very large, very fast.
items.detail: The move from intimate family comedy into Vexley’s full simulation-world takeover is a meaningful scale jump, and it changes the movie’s visual and tonal demands in the back half. That’s not a deal-breaker, but it does make the final stretch more expensive and more dependent on execution than the opening hour suggests.

items.area: Frank’s rules are still doing a lot of work.
items.detail: The tablet/code connection, the self-rewriting AI, the matter-building, and the well-being meter all arrive in layers, and the audience has to keep accepting new mechanics as the story escalates. The premise is fun, but the buyer conversation will include how much rule-explaining the movie can sustain before it starts feeling over-engineered.

items.area: The family conflict is broad by design.
items.detail: John’s workaholism and Sarah’s frustration are clear, but the marital tension is expressed in fairly familiar beats: missed promises, arguments, and the kid feeling unseen. That makes the emotional lane accessible, but it also means the script is leaning on execution and casting rather than surprise to make the adult drama feel premium.

items.area: The branded-world references narrow clearance work.
items.detail: The script leans on Fishing Planet as licensed IP and also uses a number of named brands and platforms in dialogue and action, including Target, Lyft, LinkedIn, YouTube, TikTok, Rolex, and Ozempic. None of that is fatal, but it means business affairs will want a clean pass on the IP chain and the trademark usage before anyone gets comfortable.

items.area: The child ensemble raises the casting bar.
items.detail: Ethan, Jen, Trevor, and Livvy all need to feel distinct and playable, and the movie depends on their chemistry in both comedy and emotional scenes. That’s a real strength on the page, but it also means the casting process has to find kids who can carry dialogue, timing, and ensemble rhythm without flattening into types.

issues.headline: The script is commercially legible and emotionally warm, but the back half expands into a much bigger VFX-and-world-building proposition than the setup implies. The other real conversations are clearance on the game/IP and whether the family drama can feel fresh enough to justify the scale of the fantasy swing.
